title: The Compassion of No-self and Emptiness
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Ken McLeod's An Arrow to the Heart, a commentary on the Heart Sutra, to point toward no-self and emptiness, which Kanho says words can only gesture at. Kanho pictures meeting life as standing on a beach and asking an incoming wave set to wait while emails get answered. Biting a ripe strawberry and jumping into a cold river show what living without the "me filter" feels like. Kanho also chants the Heart Sutra in its long form, naming each of the five aggregates in turn. Kanho closes with Bodhidharma's meeting with Emperor Wu, where "No merit" and "I don't know" leave the Emperor baffled, and Master Chi says that even the whole country could not bring Bodhidharma back.
topics: The Compassion of No Self and Impermanence
Ken McLeod's An Arrow to the Heart

sentences.text: Good morning.
Thank you for coming here on this smoky Sunday.
The sun has been this amazing orange; like they say, some pollution makes for beautiful sunrises and sunsets.
The working title for the talk was *The Compassion of No Self and Impermanence*.
While I was writing the talk, I realized that there really is no way of actually saying it or explaining it, so the only thing I can do is point towards it.
I trust that in the conversation following the talk, we will come closer to actually expressing it than me just sitting here and telling you what I think.
You take a seat, and your eyes meet.
Question, answer, weave together.
Inside, outside, fade away.
That's it; it echoes in timeless space.
Everything and nothing have changed.
You lost now.
That's how it goes.
Sutra, sutra.
Let's just say it holds things together.
The Tibetans chose the word *do*, a crossroad where things meet.
This meeting is a mystery; something took place, but you can't put it in words—no one can.
That's why it is called a transmission outside the sutras.
You look at your world—friends, family, home, work, and play—everything's there, just as before, and yet, not just as before.
You are no longer at ease in the old dispensation.
Now, what do you do?
This is from Ken McLeod's book, *An Arrow to the Heart*, a commentary on the Heart Sutra.
So, the compassion of no self and impermanence.
Meeting life is like standing on a beach, and I say, I see a big wave set coming my way.
I will hold up a hand and say, "Excuse me, wave, I need to handle a crisis, answer two emails, and organize my life."
Then I will deal with you.
That works very well, because the second or third wave will get me; I'll drown, and there will be no more problems.
From the beginning, the wave set was not the problem, nor was it the email or the crisis.
It was myself—myself having the expectation that the world is on hold while I sort out what is going on.
Me over here, you over there, the wave straight ahead.
No.
No, this is not what intrasnet looks like.
Life is biting into the ripe strawberry, and all your mouth knows at that moment is strawberryness.

It is jumping off the rock into the river, and all there is is wet and cold, filtered light above and touching gravel with your feet until you break back through the surface again into sunlight and air.
Wisdom—such a heavy word.
No one can carry it; everybody has it, but few know it.
You say you can't talk about it, and you are right; that's the point.
Again, from Ken McLeod's *Arrow to the Heart*.
If we live the life we think we should be living, we fail at this grand endeavor.
We are stuck in the ordinary and in what we can imagine.
The only way to escape this smallness is to, as the old Zen masters used to say, drop your skin and become one with the universe.
And this I absolutely cannot do through changing.
I cannot take what is and change it to get from here to there.
And you know what they say, when you get there, there's no there.
Change from me to free through change is putting the mind that keeps me trapped in charge of breaking me out.
Albert Einstein said, "We cannot solve our problems with the same thinking we use when we created them."
There is another way.
That way is not change; it is transformation.
It is an utter leap of faith.
It is the Heart Sutra.
It is no self.
It is dancing with impermanence, seeing the five aggregates as empty.
Empty of what?
Self-nature.
It means leaving conditioning and blinders behind and going off into the world of reality.
Forget about looking; that's how you keep your distance.
To see, you have to step into the jaws of experience, true and be true until nothing is left.
Again, Ken McLeod, *An Arrow to the Heart*.
So, we have finally arrived at the word emptiness.
We often chant the Heart Sutra in our services here in the hall, and we compress it a little bit.
So when we chant the sutra, it sounds like this: *Form does not differ from emptiness.
Emptiness does not differ from form.
Form itself is emptiness.
Emptiness itself form.
Sensations, perceptions, formations, and consciousness are also like this.* This time, I thought I'd fill in the blanks for each aggregate and do the long form: *Form does not differ from emptiness.
Emptiness does not differ from form.
Form itself is emptiness.
Emptiness itself form.
Sensation does not differ from emptiness.
Emptiness does not differ from sensation.
Sensation itself is emptiness.
Emptiness itself sensation.
Perception does not differ from emptiness.
Emptiness does not differ from perception.
Perception itself is emptiness.
Emptiness itself perception.
Formation does not differ from emptiness.
Emptiness does not differ from formation.
Formation itself is emptiness.
Emptiness itself, formation.
Consciousness does not differ from emptiness.
Emptiness does not differ from consciousness.
Consciousness itself is emptiness.
Emptiness itself, consciousness.* This says that all experience is emptiness, is boundlessness, which is the same thing.
It is unbound, it is free.
It is not defined; it is not complete or incomplete.
Everything just is.
Everything just is as it is.
Now let's talk about the extra we add: conditioning, beliefs, thoughts.
Conditioning and beliefs may whisper and tell me what I can or cannot do or what I can and cannot say.
These whispers, remember, they are conditioning and the past.
And beliefs are so persuasive.
Usually, they have an audience of one: me, me, me—that's the focus.
Me, watching out for what's mine, control everything.
But I can't; I can't control it.
I can't control my health or my age.
I can't control the weather, the smoke, the universe.
But do I really want to?
To circle back to the beginning of the talk: if we live the life we think we should be living, we fail at this grand endeavor.
We are stuck in the ordinary and in what we can imagine.
It is only when I open myself to the boundlessness or emptiness and I do not see life and the universe through the me filter that I can get somewhere unexpected.
That I can be open for the moment of Zen or grace or whatever I may call it, to feel for and with all beings.
Norman Fischer once wrote, "This moment of compassion, true altruism is not self-sacrifice for the benefit of others, a guilt-driven sense that we should be good.
We should be nice.
We should be kind."
It is the profound recognition that self and other are not fundamentally different, only apparently different.
It is the recognition that this I lives because you are alive.
In the middle of everything changing so fast it wants to make my head spin, that is life and love.
And looking around the world becomes precious to my eyes.
In this spirit, I would like to end the talk with a story of Bodhidharma's meeting with Emperor Wu.
Bodhidharma, a great Buddhist master from India, arrived at the court of Emperor Wu in southern China in the sixth century CE.
Emperor Wu was a great patron of Buddhism and a sincere devotee.
He had sponsored many monasteries and sutra translations and the ordination of many monks.
The Emperor asked Bodhidharma what merit he had accrued by all these good works.
Bodhidharma unhesitatingly replied, "No merit."
Startled, the Emperor asked, "What is the highest meaning of the sacred truth?"
Bodhidharma said, "Vast emptiness, nothing holy."
The Emperor asked, "Who is facing me?"
Bodhidharma said, "I don't know."
The Emperor did not understand.
Bodhidharma departed and crossed the Yangtze River to the Kingdom of Wei in northern China.
Emperor Wu asked his spiritual advisor Master Chi about Bodhidharma.
Master Chi said that this Indian monk was Avalokiteshvara, the Bodhisattva of compassion.
Transmitting the Buddha mind seal, the Emperor felt regret and wanted to send a tentance to bring Bodhidharma back.
Master Chi said, "Don't say you will send someone to fetch him.
Even if everyone in the whole country were to go after him, he still would not return."
If something in this talk resonated with you, you may wish to investigate it further.
If it did not speak to you, please forget it right now.
